name: Lena Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Lena, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I like talking about this, my husband says I never stop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Marlow Yates, a firm of about twenty-five people that does accounts and tax for restaurants, bakeries and family shops. I've set up most of our AI: it reads the till reports and supplier invoices, and I check the drafts and chase the gaps. I'm fast but I still make real mistakes on the technical side, like stock valuation for a restaurant, so Mr Yates checks me closely. The best part is sitting with a family who've run a bakery for thirty years and showing them, on one page, which loaves actually make money. Kerem, my husband, runs his family's furniture workshop, so I hear about wood all evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have put a lot of effort into something small. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that people oversold, and I'd keep using it. I'd post a short note about which tools are actually worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes very little for me, because I already use it for the routine bits. My job's safe, the firm's busy, and families will always need someone to do their books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, get my exams done by next autumn, and keep using AI every day. I'd also spend a few evenings a month sorting out the books for Kerem's workshop, which are a mess. We'd keep saving, we've got about a year's costs plus our share of the workshop building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Mostly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the mess in the workshop's books?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerem's father keeps everything in a notebook and a shoebox. My father-in-law is a brilliant craftsman and terrible with paper. I'd set up a simple system with an AI tool reading the receipts, and he'd grumble for a month and then love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else on your mind outside AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wanting children in a year or two, and making sure we can afford for me to go part-time. My mother stayed home with us and I'd like to do some of that.

say: I'd call AI a good tool that people **oversold**.
I'd post about which tools are worth **paying for**.
think: It changes little, since I already use it for **routine bits**.
My job's **safe**, because families always need their books done.
do: Set up **AI receipt-reading** for my husband's family workshop.
Keep **saving**, with a year's costs plus our share of the workshop building.
S0.quote: My father-in-law is a brilliant craftsman and terrible with paper.
fieldNote: She's **secure**: a year's savings, a property share and a busy firm.
She sees AI as **routine help**, already built into her day.
Her plans tie **work and family**: children and part-time work soon.

steps.text: Finish the professional exams by next autumn
Set up AI receipt reading for the family furniture workshop
Keep a year's savings alongside the workshop building share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I think is happening. I'd be right in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, and people who learn and work hard will be fine. I'd say businesses should be free to use it, and families should help each other through. I'd be positive about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay, because I'm the one who sets it up at Marlow Yates. But the junior checking work is shrinking. If I'm only good at setting tools up, a cheaper tool will set itself up soon, so I'd want something I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Mr Yates to let me build a service for small family businesses, monthly books done by AI and checked by me, at a fixed price. I'd start doing the same on the side for three or four families from our community. And I'd put some savings into Kerem's workshop for new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. I'd see the opportunity before I saw the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mr Yates mind you doing work on the side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if it's his kind of client. I'd only take families who'd never pay a firm's fees anyway, like my aunt's corner shop. I'd tell him straight, I'm not one for hiding things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about colleagues who don't like the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, the other junior, hates it. I'd show him, but I wouldn't carry him. People have to want to learn.

say: I'd say hard workers who **learn** will be fine.
I'd say businesses should be **free** to use AI, and families should **help each other**.
think: I'm okay because I **set up the tools** at my firm.
A cheaper tool will **set itself up** soon, so I want something I **own**.
do: Propose a **fixed-price** AI bookkeeping service for family businesses at my firm.
Do books on the side for **three or four** community families.
Put savings into my husband's **workshop machines**.
feel: **Uneasy** but in a good way, seeing **opportunity** before risk.
S1.quote: If I'm only good at setting tools up, a cheaper tool will set itself up soon, so I'd want something I own.
fieldNote: Her **own job** looks safe for now, so uneasy, not anxious.
She wants **ownership**, not just skills, a free-market instinct.
She is firm that colleagues must **want to learn**; she won't carry them.

steps.text: Pitch a fixed-price AI bookkeeping service to the firm's partner
Keep the books for four community families on the side
Put savings into new machines for the furniture workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a different thing altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge change and families will need to stick together, and that the government shouldn't try to stop it but should keep things orderly. I'd say it plainly at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone, and soon. If AI can do any thinking work, it doesn't need me to set it up or check it. But Kerem's workshop is hands-on, and furniture made by hand has about three years before the robots, maybe more because people pay for a craftsman's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Marlow Yates within the year and go into the workshop full-time, running the finances, the website and the sales with AI. I'd put about fifteen thousand of our savings into a bigger showroom space. We'd still try for a baby, because Kerem's family would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but the whole household would be resting on one workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't putting savings in the workshop risky if robots come in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's risky. Robots making chairs in a factory isn't the same as a family workshop with a name, and people still pay extra for handmade. I'd sell that story hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my father I'm leaving accounting for a furniture business, and he'd worry. Then I'd show him the numbers, and he'd come round. He ran a shop for twenty years.

say: I'd say **families** must stick together and **government** should keep things orderly.
think: My job is **gone soon**, since AGI doesn't need me to check it.
Handmade furniture has about **three years** before robots, maybe more for a **name**.
do: Leave the firm within the year to **run the workshop's** finances and sales.
Put about **fifteen thousand** of savings into a bigger showroom.
Still try for a **baby**, with family help.
feel: **Anxious**, with the household resting on **one workshop**.
S2.quote: Robots making chairs in a factory isn't the same as a family workshop with a name, and people still pay extra for handmade.
fieldNote: She expects her **job to go** but has a concrete plan, so anxious.
She stakes the household on the **family workshop** and the **robot gap**.
Family support lets her keep **children** in the plan.

steps.text: Leave the accounting firm within a year for the family workshop
Put fifteen thousand of savings into a bigger showroom
Try for a baby with family help nearby
Run the workshop's sales and website with AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build the workshop side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast, but people who start preparing now will be fine. I'd tell friends to learn a craft or own a small business, not just hold a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose the accounting job around 2031, but I'd have years to grow the workshop first. The robots arrive in 2034, so the workshop would have three more years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Marlow Yates and qualify, while building the workshop's online sales in the evenings. By 2028 I'd go part-time at the firm and half-time in the workshop. We'd have our first child around 2027.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy to anxious. Mostly I'd feel busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the workshop look like by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper showroom, online orders, two apprentices, and Kerem's father still in the corner doing the carving. I'd be running everything that isn't wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how Kerem learned and how his father learned. I'd rather train two young people than hire one more machine, because that's how a family business should grow.

say: I'd say people who **prepare now** will be fine.
I'd tell friends to learn a **craft** or own a **small business**.
think: I'd lose the accounting job around **2031**.
The workshop gets years to grow, plus **three more** after robots.
do: Qualify while building **online sales** in the evenings.
Take on **two apprentices** and have a first child around 2027.
S3.quote: I'd rather train two young people than hire one more machine, because that's how a family business should grow.
fieldNote: She still expects to lose the **accounting job**, so anxious overall.
Despite being an AI user, she'd hire **apprentices**, reflecting traditional values.
Five years lets her **phase** the switch gradually.

steps.text: Build the workshop's online sales in the evenings
Take on two apprentices at the workshop by 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a comfortable amount of time, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for people who want to work, and I'd say it confidently at work. I'd say we should have more apprenticeships, not more benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a long run as an accountant, maybe even buy into Marlow Yates as a partner, and still build the workshop on the side. My job is all thinking, so 2036 is my date. The workshop runs to 2039 and maybe beyond.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, push for a senior role, and use AI to do the work of two people. I'd put money into the workshop every year and help it grow online. We'd have two children and I'd go part-time for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. It feels like enough time to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay an accountant until 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not all the way. Around 2032 I'd move into the workshop full-time, before my job disappears under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents getting older, and making sure the workshop isn't the only basket. But ten years is enough to build two baskets, so the workshop isn't the only one.

say: I'd call ten years **plenty** for people who want to work.
think: My job is all thinking, so **2036** is my date.
The **workshop** runs to 2039 and maybe beyond.
do: Push for a **senior role**, using AI to do the work of two.
Put money into the **workshop** every year.
feel: **Uneasy** at most, with **enough time** to do things properly.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to build two baskets, so the workshop isn't the only one.
fieldNote: She sees the household's income as **safe** with a growing workshop, so uneasy.
She'd leave accounting **before** it disappears, by her own timing.
Ageing **parents** are a quiet worry she raises unprompted.

steps.text: Use AI to do the work of two in a senior role
Put money into the furniture workshop every year
Have two children and go part-time for a few years
Move to the workshop full-time around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would push us into the workshop before it's ready. What would help is apprenticeships for small firms, and banks lending to family businesses that want to grow instead of to big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people still value a name. If everything is made by machines, the family name on the workshop is the one thing a robot can't copy.

headlineQuote: If everything is made by machines, the family name on the workshop is the one thing a robot can't copy.
portrait: Lena is a **junior accountant** at a twenty-five-person firm serving restaurants, bakeries and family shops.
She set up most of the firm's **AI** and uses it daily, though she still makes **technical mistakes**.
She's married to Kerem, who runs his family's **furniture workshop**, and has strong savings.
She moves from calm to **anxious**, betting on **ownership** and the family business.
Her traditional values show in favouring **apprentices** over machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, forcing the workshop to carry the family **too soon**.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for small firms and **bank lending** to family businesses.
